orchestrator_causes: The entrepreneur loses money because she buys bales blind from suppliers who misrepresent quality — the problem is a lack of trusted supply channels and grading information before purchase.

The entrepreneur loses money because she cannot predict which styles and brands her customers actually want — the problem is that even good-quality bales contain stock she can't sell, meaning her demand-reading skill, not her sourcing, is the gap.

The entrepreneur loses money because in a saturated Owino market where the next stall sells identical dresses, her margins are already so thin that a single bad bale wipes out her cushion — the problem is competitive price erosion leaving no buffer to absorb normal sourcing variance.
raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** Your money problem starts before you even open the bale. You told me yourself that you pay 500,000 for a bale but "cannot see inside properly," and half of it turns out torn or old-fashioned. That means you are buying blind, trusting suppliers who have no reason to tell you the truth about what is packed inside.

**PREDICTION:** If this is your real problem, you should notice that the same supplier gives you good bales sometimes and bad ones other times, with no way to tell in advance. Traders who buy from a known, trusted source will report far fewer "surprise" losses than you do.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be finding one or two suppliers who let you inspect or grade bales before paying, even if their price is a bit higher. Ask other Owino sellers which importers give honest, consistent bales, and start building a steady relationship with those, instead of buying from whoever is nearest.

The cash flow problem exists because his 5-10% margin is too thin to build any buffer, since bigger importers undercut his buying price — the issue is that he occupies a losing position in the supply chain, not how he collects payments.

The cash flow problem exists because he competes on identical commodity plastics where he has no reason to command better terms or loyalty, so customers freely delay him and suppliers demand cash — the issue is undifferentiation that leaves him with zero bargaining power on both ends.
raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** Your own words say it clearly. Your money is "on paper but no cash to restock." You sell mostly cash, but the credit you give to upcountry shopkeepers from Masaka, Mbarara and the DRC side comes back slowly, and meanwhile your suppliers "want cash upfront." That gap, money stuck out there while stock money is needed now, is what leaves you unable to grab good deals.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you should see that when you add up what customers still owe you, that amount is roughly the same size as the stock money you keep saying you are short of. The days you miss import deals will line up with the days big credit payments are late.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be tightening how you give and collect credit. Write down every customer's balance and due date, set a firm short limit (say 7 days), stop new credit to anyone still owing, and call late payers the day they pass the date.

The previous advisor treats this as a collection timing problem, but even if every customer paid on the dot, you would still be trapped because your margin is too thin to ever get ahead of the big importers.

**CAUSE:** You said it yourself. "Some of the big guys import container loads so they sell cheaper than I even buy." Your 5 to 10 percent margin is so thin that one slow payment wipes out your buffer, and you can never save enough to grab the good deals. The real trouble is where you sit in the chain, buying from importers who also compete against you, so you are squeezed from both sides.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that even in weeks when customers pay you on time, you still cannot build a real cash reserve, because the margin per carton is just too small to grow.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be changing your buying position. Team up with other Kikuubo wholesalers to place one big container order together so you buy at the importer price instead of buying from the people who undercut you.

Both advisors miss the deeper reason your money moves the way it does. Diagnosis 1 treats it as paperwork and timing, and Diagnosis 2 treats it as your buying position, but neither explains WHY customers feel free to delay you and suppliers feel free to demand cash from you in the first place.

**CAUSE:** You told me Kikuubo is "packed with people selling exactly the same plastics" and the fight is only on price. When your buckets and basins are identical to everyone else's, no customer has a reason to pay you promptly or stay loyal, and no supplier has a reason to trust you with stock. You have nothing that makes you worth better treatment, so both sides squeeze you.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice your late-paying customers also buy from other wholesalers, and they never fear losing you because they can get the same goods next door.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be giving upcountry customers a reason to stick with you only, like reliable stock of one item nobody else keeps steadily, so they protect the relationship by paying on time.

orchestrator_causes: The entrepreneur buys stock by guessing rather than tracking which sizes and styles actually sell, so her capital keeps landing on unwanted pairs — the problem is lack of sales data, not the shoes themselves.

Her cash is permanently trapped because her sales are only strong at school-opening and festive seasons, meaning she buys big but sells in bursts — the problem is a mismatch between her purchasing rhythm and her seasonal demand, not which styles she picks.

The slow shoes aren't selling because arcade shops have pulled the style-conscious customers away, leaving her holding stock the market no longer wants at any price — the problem is shifting customer preference toward "fancy" imports, not her buying choices.
raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** In your own words, you "bought many pairs in sizes and styles that customers are not asking for" while running out of the fast-moving sizes. That happened because you buy by guessing instead of writing down which sizes and styles actually sell. The shoes are fine, the problem is you have no record telling you what to restock, so your capital keeps landing on the wrong pairs.

**PREDICTION:** If this is the real cause, you should see that the shoes sitting unsold are the ones you never checked before buying, while the pairs that vanish fast (certain children's sizes at school opening, popular ladies' styles for weddings) are the ones you keep running short on.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to start a simple notebook where you write down every pair you sell, the size, the style, and when it went. After a few weeks that record will tell you exactly what to buy more of, so your next purchases match real demand instead of guesswork.

The previous advisor blames your record-keeping, but that misses that even the right shoes will sit if you buy them all at once and only sell in two short bursts a year.

**CAUSE:** You told me your sales "spike at school opening and festive seasons but are slow in between." That is the heart of it. You buy big amounts at once, but customers only come in bursts, so your cash gets locked in shoes for months waiting for the next school term or wedding season. The problem is not which styles you picked, it is that your buying happens in one lump while your selling is spread thin across a long slow period.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you should notice that even your good, popular pairs sit for weeks or months during the quiet time between seasons, not just the odd sizes.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to buy in smaller batches timed close to each busy season, so less cash sits frozen during the slow months and you keep some free to restock fast movers.

Both previous advisors miss what you already told me plainly, that the arcade shops "look fancy so some customers prefer them." A better notebook or smaller batches will not help if buyers have simply stopped wanting the plain style you sell.

**CAUSE:** The slow shoes are not moving because the new arcade shops have pulled away your style-conscious customers with their "fancy" imported look. You said yourself that even though your shoes are "cheaper and good," some people now prefer the arcade ones. That means the market has shifted taste, so those pairs sit unsold not because of your sizes or your seasons, but because the demand for that plain style has walked out the door.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will see the shoes that stick are the plainer, older-looking styles, while anything close to the arcade look sells even in odd sizes.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to walk through the arcades, see exactly which styles are pulling customers, and stock a few of those fashionable looks at your cheaper price.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be requiring a small mobile money deposit before you reserve or send anything, exactly as you were already thinking. Make the deposit count toward the final price so serious buyers lose nothing, but time-wasters have to put real money down before you move.

**CAUSE:** You told me yourself that goods "bring more but slowly" while you earn only "small margins" on them. It is not the credit that breaks you, it is that the goods business earns too little per item to absorb any delay at all.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that even when almost everyone pays on time, you still feel squeezed and cannot build up spare cash from the shop side alone.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to check the actual profit on each good and raise prices or drop the low-margin, slow items, so every sale earns enough to survive a late payment.

orchestrator_causes: The entrepreneur is losing capital because he prices and tracks profit in shillings while his costs are in dollars, so currency movement erodes him invisibly — the problem is a lack of a pricing/accounting system that accounts for the dollar, not the market itself.

The entrepreneur cannot pass on rising costs because thin-margin phones dominate his sales in a price-transparent market where customers instantly compare — the problem is his product mix and competitive position, not currency management.

The entrepreneur is exposed to the rate because he holds inventory across time and buys after selling, so any delay lets the shilling weaken against him — the problem is his cash and stock timing, not pricing or product choice.
raw_diagnoses:

In your own words, "I think I made a profit but when I go to restock I realise I actually can't afford the same quantity." That is not the market beating you, that is your accounting hiding the true cost of your stock.

**PREDICTION:** If this is correct, you will notice that your shilling cash pile looks fine or even growing, yet the number of phones or speakers you can buy back keeps shrinking each time you restock.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to record every item's cost in dollars, and each time you sell, set your shilling price using today's rate plus a small buffer, then check whether your sale covers replacing that item in dollars, not just whether the shilling number looks bigger.

The previous advisor treats this as a bookkeeping trick, but even perfect dollar accounting cannot save you if your best-selling product simply has no room to absorb any cost increase.

**CAUSE:** The reason you cannot pass rising costs onto customers is that phones dominate your sales, and by your own words their "margins are thin because of competition" in a place where "prices are almost the same everywhere because customers compare quickly." When the dollar moves, you have no cushion to raise phone prices because the buyer next door will undercut you instantly, so your capital gets squeezed.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that when you try to add even a small amount to a phone price, walk-in customers walk away or haggle you back down, while your accessories (better margin) sell without the same fight.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be shifting your money toward accessories and higher-margin items where customers do not compare so sharply, so a rising dollar eats into profit you actually have instead of wiping out capital.

Both advisors miss it. The first treats this as a counting mistake, but you already see the loss clearly, you just see it too late. The second blames thin phone margins, but even fat margins get eaten if you hold stock while the shilling slides.

**CAUSE:** Your real exposure is timing. You buy in dollars, hold stock, then buy again after selling, so every day between selling and restocking is a day the shilling can weaken against you. In your words, "by the time I sell in shillings, the dollar has sometimes gone up." The gap between your cash coming in and your restocking going out is where your capital quietly leaks.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, the items that sit longest before selling will hurt you most, while anything you sell and restock the same week barely loses value even when the rate moves.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to shorten the gap between selling and restocking, and hold a small dollar reserve so you can restock immediately at the old rate instead of waiting for shilling cash to pile up first.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be shifting more of your borrowed money into non-perishable items (tools, storage bags, irrigation parts) that survive a failed season and can be sold the next one.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to test your self-mixing plan on a small batch first. Buy maize and silverfish, mix feed for a small group of birds, and carefully compare the cost per tray and their laying against the birds on commercial feed before switching the whole flock.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to stagger your pond stocking so you harvest something small every month, and start smoking part of each harvest so you can sell it slowly and bring in steady cash between the big fresh sales. This turns your lumpy income into a regular flow that covers weekly feed.

The previous advisor treated this as a timing problem, but staggering harvests will not help if you simply do not have enough cash saved to feed the fish through any single growing cycle.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you should see that if you add up all the feed money for one pond over four months, it is more than the cash you ever have in hand at the start of that cycle.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to work out the exact feed cost to grow one pond to full size, then hold that full amount in savings before you stock, or lower feed cost by making some feed yourself.

You are following the same natural calendar as every other Mbale farmer, so your tomatoes and cabbages hit the market in the very same week that everyone else's do, and the flood of supply crushes the price. **CAUSE:** You said it yourself, when there are plenty of tomatoes "we practically give them away because they'll rot otherwise." The real trap is that you cannot store anything, so the moment your crop is ready you must sell at whatever price exists that day. Even if you plant off-season, one good harvest week will still force you to dump everything before it spoils.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that the days you are forced to sell fastest are the days you get the worst prices, and produce you could have held even a week would have fetched much more.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be building simple storage and preservation, like drying tomatoes and sukuma wiki or a cool store for cabbages, so you can hold stock and release it slowly when prices recover.

Both previous advisors focus on *when* you sell (timing) or *how long* you can hold your crop (storage), but they miss that even off-season or stored tomatoes are still just plain tomatoes, the same ones every other farmer has. As long as your product looks identical to everyone else's, you take whatever price the market gives.

**CAUSE:** You told me many farmers around Mbale grow the exact same vegetables, so buyers see no difference between your tomatoes and anyone else's. That is why traders set the price and you accept it. Until your product stands apart (a graded, sorted, packed, or processed item, or a buyer who has agreed to take yours specifically), you will always be a price-taker, even in the off-season.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that even when you bring good clean produce, no buyer pays you extra for quality, they pay the same flat market rate as the person next to you selling ordinary stock.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to differentiate, sort and grade your best tomatoes into a premium pack, or lock in a standing supply deal with one or two restaurants who buy your eggs already, so you have a buyer and a price agreed before harvest.

**CAUSE:** You told me your mushrooms "spoil in two or three days" because you "sometimes harvest more than I can sell." That is not a demand problem, it is a timing problem. When a shopkeeper cannot tell your egg apart from anyone else's, the only thing they haggle over is price, so you have no way to charge more when your feed costs climb. That is why your margin gets "squeezed from both sides," even though the families who come to your farm already value your eggs because "they know my eggs are fresh."

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that the families buying directly from your farm rarely argue about price, while the market shopkeepers drop you the moment cheaper trays appear.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be turning that freshness reputation into something buyers can see and pay extra for, like dated, branded trays sold straight to restaurants and families who care about quality, instead of competing tray-for-tray in the flooded market.

The core problem is that everyone is trapped in the same low-value commodity at the same moment — since all farmers grow identical potatoes on the same harvest calendar, the only real escape is differentiation through timing, variety, or product form, not storing or grouping around the same undifferentiated crop.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be building that simple ventilated store you mentioned, and testing it carefully. Store a measured batch, track how many weeks they stay good and what price you get, so you know exactly how much storage time buys you before rot sets in.

**CAUSE:** The real issue is that every farmer negotiates by himself while the Kampala traders come as a small, coordinated group. **PREDICTION:** If this is the core problem, you should notice that even the farmers who do have storage or better quality potatoes still get squeezed to nearly the same low price, because each one is still bargaining alone against the same truck buyers.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be finishing that farmer group you mentioned and agreeing on one shared minimum price before the traders arrive, so you sell as one large block instead of many desperate individuals.

Both advisors accept the same trap you are stuck in, they just argue about how to survive inside it. Storage lets you wait a few weeks and grouping lets you bargain harder, but both still sell the exact same ordinary potato that every other farmer floods the market with on the same day.

**CAUSE:** The deeper problem is in your own words, "every farmer here grows Irish potatoes, so at harvest time everyone is selling at once." You are competing on a crop that is identical to everyone else's, harvested on the same calendar, so the traders can always find another desperate seller. Nothing you do to store or group changes the fact that you are one of hundreds selling the same thing at the same moment.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you should see that whenever a farmer offers something different (an early or late variety, washed and graded potatoes, or peeled chips) they get a noticeably better price and are not squeezed like the rest.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be breaking away from the crowd by testing one difference, an off-season planting or turning some potatoes into washed, graded, or ready-cut product that traders and restaurants will pay more for.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be staggering your four ponds so one matures roughly every two months, giving you a smaller harvest income steadily through the year that covers ongoing feed costs without borrowing. Start by stocking each pond on a rolling schedule instead of all together.

**CAUSE:** You said "a big chunk of the harvest money goes to repaying debts" and you "never build up capital to expand." That is not just a timing issue, it means each fish is costing you almost as much to raise as it sells for. With cheap wild fish from Lake Victoria and frozen imports pushing your prices down, and feed running for six to eight months, your profit per fish is simply too small to leave a surplus.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be adding a faster-earning stream now, like raising and selling fingerlings to other farmers or smoking and drying fish to sell to your market women, so money comes in monthly instead of only at harvest.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be getting the bus timetable directly from the drivers and stage workers you already serve. Ask them each evening which buses are expected the next morning, and write it down so you can match your cooking to the travelers coming.

**PREDICTION:** If this is the real cause, you will notice that even on days you guessed the crowd right, you still either had leftovers or long waits, because one big pot cannot bend to how people actually arrive.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to test one or two new suppliers by ordering a small batch of screens from each, installing them, and tracking how many come back as faulty over a month. Whichever supplier gives you the fewest returns becomes your main source, even if you pay a bit more.

**CAUSE:** You said yourself there are salons "on almost every corner" and new ones open offering "very low prices to pull customers." **NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be giving customers one clear reason to choose you that has nothing to do with price, like a signature style, faster service, or a comfort touch others do not offer, so they stop comparing you on cost alone.

Both previous advisors focus on your salon and your styles, but the pattern you describe (packed weekends and month-end, empty weekdays) matches your customers' pay cycle, not your service quality or the crowded market. **CAUSE:** You told me your customers are market women and young ladies who come "especially on weekends and month end when they have been paid." **NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be offering a small "pay later" or save-with-me arrangement so customers can book weekday slots and settle at month-end.

raw_diagnoses:

You said clients pay "a small deposit then expect me to buy everything and finish the function before paying the balance," which means you are personally financing every event with your own or borrowed cash. When one client delays the balance for weeks, your capital is stuck and you cannot take the next job, so your terms are quietly forcing you to be the bank.

**PREDICTION:** If this is the true cause, you should notice that the functions that squeeze you hardest are the ones with the smallest upfront deposits, and that clients who pay more before the event almost never leave you struggling.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be changing your contract so clients pay enough before the function to fully cover ingredients (for example 70 percent upfront), with the balance due on the event day, not weeks later. Put it in writing before you accept any booking.

**CAUSE:** The real issue is that you have no money set aside separate from what each function needs. You said "I'm always using my own money or borrowing to fund functions, and when a client delays payment I can't take the next job because my capital is stuck." That means your entire operation runs on the exact amount one function costs, so any single delay freezes everything. Even if you demand more upfront, one slow client still stops you cold when you have no buffer.

**PREDICTION:** If this is the real cause, you'll notice that even functions where clients paid a good deposit still leave you unable to start the next job whenever a previous balance is late, because there is no separate reserve to draw from.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be building that working capital reserve you mentioned, setting aside a fixed share of profit from each function until you can fund one full event without borrowing.

**CAUSE:** The reason clients hold your balance for weeks is that you have no name that scares them. You said the "more established with bigger names" get the big-budget clients, while you "mostly get the medium and smaller functions" that come through referrals. When a client knows you fought to win the job and depend on the referral, they know you will not push back, so they pay late because they can.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that when a well-known client or a repeat client who respects your reputation hires you, they pay on time, while the loosely referred medium clients are the ones who drag payment.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be building a visible reputation (photos of your functions, testimonials, a recognizable name) so clients see you as a caterer they cannot mess around, not a favor they can delay.

The slow months are genuinely low-demand for custom sewing because walk-in repair and ready-made buyers have shifted to cheaper imported finished clothes, so the quiet stretches reflect a shrinking base of routine year-round customers, not merely event timing.
raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** Every single thing you make is tied to a date on the calendar. Dresses and gomesi for functions, school uniforms for term openings. When you say "it depends on functions and school terms," that is the whole trouble. You have nothing that people need in the ordinary months when no one is getting married and no schools are opening, so your income comes in waves and then dries up.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that your quiet months line up exactly with the gaps between wedding season and school term openings, and that even your walk-in repairs are not enough to fill those empty weeks.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be building one steady, everyday product that people buy all year regardless of the calendar, like simple work clothes, market aprons, uniforms for shops and hotels, or a repairs-and-alterations service you actively advertise. That gives you money flowing in during the months functions and schools cannot.

orchestrator_causes: The business is trying to own a physical rental asset (tents, chairs) whose demand is inherently lumpy and concentrated on weekends, so idle-capacity economics make in-house ownership the wrong model — the problem is asset ownership, not capacity sizing.

Her bookings cluster on the same Saturdays because she isn't actively steering customers toward less-contested dates through pricing or scheduling incentives — the problem is unmanaged demand timing, not a shortage of equipment.

She is bundling two different businesses (high-margin catering and low-margin equipment rental) that compete for the same limited weekend attention, so spreading herself across both is what causes the overbooking crunch — the problem is lack of focus, not capacity or demand.
raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** The real problem is that you are trying to own tents and chairs, which is the wrong thing to own. You said it yourself, you "can't buy more equipment for peak days because it would just sit idle on the slow weekends." Equipment that only earns money on Saturdays but costs you storage and cash all week long is a bad asset to own, no matter how you size it.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that your owned tents and chairs sit unused most days of the week, and even in a good month the rental fees barely cover what that equipment cost you to buy and store.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to stop buying equipment and instead lock in a solid, priced partnership with a dedicated tent company, so you rent everything you need per event and put all your cash into the catering side where your margins are strongest. Let someone else carry the idle equipment.

The previous advisor treats this as an ownership problem, but that misses that even a rental partner won't save you when every client wants the exact same Saturday and you're scrambling to serve them all at once.

**CAUSE:** Your real trouble is that all your bookings pile onto the same few Saturdays because you take dates as customers request them, without nudging anyone toward quieter weekends. You said you sometimes get "two weddings on one Saturday" and must "turn down business or rush to rent more," which shows the issue is timing, not just how many chairs you own.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that your calendar has a handful of jammed Saturdays alongside plenty of empty or half-empty weekends every month, and your equipment sits idle on those slow dates.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to spread demand by offering a discount or free extra (say a decor upgrade) for clients who book your quieter weekends, and charging a premium for the crowded peak Saturdays so fewer clients cluster there.

Both previous advisors treat this as an equipment puzzle, whether to own it or when to book it. But the real trouble is that you are running two different businesses at once, and both fight for your attention on the same busy Saturdays.

**CAUSE:** You are doing high-margin catering AND low-margin tent and chair rental, and both demand your energy on the exact same weekend hours. You said yourself the crunch comes when "two weddings on one Saturday" hit, and you are stretched thin because you are trying to cook, coordinate staff, and manage equipment all at once. The overbooking is really you being pulled in two directions, not a chair shortage.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that on your worst weekends it is your own time and attention that runs out first, not just tents, and the rental side earns you far less per hour of effort than the cooking does.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to drop the equipment rental as your own operation and focus fully on catering, partnering with a tent company so you sell only what you do best.

orchestrator_causes: The supply chain is the root problem — Charles genuinely cannot source reliable parts because his Kampala suppliers pass off fakes as genuine, so failures are unavoidable regardless of his skill or pricing.

The real problem is that customers can't distinguish quality and shop only on price, so the market rewards the cheap poor-work competitors and punishes Charles for using better parts — this is a positioning and customer-education problem, not a parts problem.

The problem is Charles's own business model — he absorbs the cost of failures by redoing work for free with no warranty terms or diagnostics that separate part failure from labour, so any defective part directly destroys his margin regardless of where he buys.
raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** Your real problem is that the Kampala suppliers are selling you fake copies dressed up as genuine screens, and you said yourself you "can't tell the fake from the real one until it fails." That is why phones come back within two months and you redo the work for free, which eats your profit. The failure is coming from the part, not from your six years of skill.

**PREDICTION:** If this is the true cause, you should notice that the parts from your two new warranty suppliers fail far less often than the cheap ones did, even though your repair method has not changed at all.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be locking down a trusted supply line. Keep records of which supplier each part came from and track how many come back, so you can see clearly which sources give genuine parts and drop the ones whose screens keep failing, even if their price looks tempting.

The previous advisor treats this as a supply problem, but even with perfect genuine parts Charles will keep losing because customers don't see the difference and just chase the lowest price.

**CAUSE:** You told me customers "go to them first and only come to me after their phone gets spoiled again," and that your better suppliers cost more so you "struggle to compete on price." That tells me the market can't tell your quality work from the cheap poor work, so price is the only thing customers judge by, and that punishes you for fitting real parts.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you'll notice that when you explain original versus copy, most customers still pick the cheaper option and only appreciate your quality after their phone fails a second time.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be making quality visible and easy to trust. Give a written warranty slip with every repair, show customers the difference between real and fake screens, and put a sign advertising "genuine parts, guaranteed" so people choose you on trust, not just price.

Both previous advisors treat this as something outside Charles's control, either the suppliers or the customers, but the truth is his own way of running the shop is what turns every bad part into his personal loss.

**CAUSE:** You said when a part fails "they blame my work, not the part, and I have to redo it for free which eats my profit." The problem is not just the fake screen, it is that you swallow the whole cost yourself. You have no warranty terms written down and no way to show the customer it was the part that failed, not your labour, so every defective screen destroys your margin no matter where you bought it.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that even when a part clearly failed on its own, you still end up paying for both the new part and the labour again, and the customer never contributes anything.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be writing a simple repair slip that separates part cost from labour, states a clear warranty period, and lets you charge for labour when only the part failed.

FAIL: Criterion 2 (action-incompatible) — Diagnoses 2 and 3 recommend effectively the same action (issuing a written warranty/repair slip), so following one addresses the other's core problem.

simulated_response: All three of them are pointing at real things, but reading them together made me see the problem differently. Then I will start tracking which supplier each screen came from, because if I keep that record for a few months I will finally know which Kampala man is selling me rubbish and I can cut him off. raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** The real problem is this one rider, not the bike or the market. Your own words prove it. Your first rider "pays well and takes care of the bike," while the second "is always behind on payment and the bike keeps breaking because he rides it carelessly." Same bike terms, same area, two completely different results. The difference is the person, not the business.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you should see that your good rider almost never misses a payment and rarely needs repairs, while the careless rider's breakdowns and missed days come in a repeating pattern month after month, no matter how many chances you give him.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to take the bike back from the careless rider and hand it to a serious replacement on the same daily hire terms. Before handing over, put the written agreement with penalties in place so the new rider knows repairs from careless riding come out of his pocket.

The previous advisor blames the individual rider, but the same loose terms let ANY future rider do the exact same thing to you, so swapping people just resets the trap.

**CAUSE:** The real weakness is how your hire deal is built. You said "when it breaks I pay for repairs but he still doesn't pay the daily fee," which means the agreement puts all the risk on you and gives you no way to force payment or protect the bike. Your good rider behaves well by luck of character, not because the deal requires it, so any careless rider will always cost you.

**PREDICTION:** If this is correct, you will notice you have no clear right to reclaim the bike or charge repairs back to the rider, and every time he falls behind you feel stuck "hoping he improves" instead of acting.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be writing a proper agreement that makes the rider pay for repairs from careless riding, sets penalties for missed days, and gives you the clear right to take the bike back after a set number of unpaid days. Apply it to both riders.

Both previous advisors assume a rider or a contract fix will solve this, but they skip the question of whether the daily fee itself is even payable now. If the app fares have dropped so low that a hardworking rider cannot cover fuel, repairs, and your daily fee all at once, then no penalty clause or replacement rider fixes the math.

**CAUSE:** You said yourself the app companies "brought in even more riders who accept low fares" and customers "compare prices on the app," which has pushed earnings down for every rider on the street. Your careless rider may genuinely be short because after fuel and wear there is simply not enough left to pay your daily rate, especially on a bike that eats repair money.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, even your good rider is quietly struggling, paying on time but skipping his own maintenance or working longer hours just to meet the same fee you set before the apps arrived.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be checking what a rider actually clears in a day now, then lowering the daily fee to a level a serious rider can truly pay while still owning the bike eventually.

orchestrator_causes: The tailor physically cannot produce enough garments to meet accepted orders because she has only one machine and shares an overlock, making this a capacity constraint that better scheduling alone won't fix.

The tailor accepts more work than she can deliver because she fears losing income and can't say no, making this a commitment-discipline problem where even added machine capacity would just get overbooked again.

The tailor lacks a reliable way to estimate how long each job actually takes and stack deadlines realistically, making this a planning-and-sequencing problem rather than a shortage of machines or willpower.
raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** Your real problem is that you simply cannot sew fast enough with one machine and an overlock you must share. You said yourself that you promise the same deadline to many people but "can't finish them all with just one machine," and you wait to share the overlock, which slows every dress down. Even perfect scheduling would not fix this, because your hands and your one machine can only produce so many garments in a day.

**PREDICTION:** If this is the cause, you will notice that even the jobs you accepted with honest, realistic dates still pile up, and you often sit idle waiting your turn on the shared overlock instead of finishing garments.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be raising your daily output. Keep saving for your own overlock as you planned, and in the meantime count how many garments you can truly finish in a week so you only accept that many orders.

The previous advisor blames the machine, but you told us the real trigger yourself, you keep promising too many people because "I fear turning away customers," so more capacity would just get filled with more overpromising.

**CAUSE:** Your own words say it plainly, "I keep overcommitting because I fear turning away customers." The bottleneck is not the machine, it is that you say yes and give the same deadline to everyone to protect today's income, then your name suffers when you cannot deliver. A second overlock would just let you overbook faster.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice that even in slow weeks, when the shared overlock is free, you still promise dates you cannot keep because you cannot bring yourself to say "not this week."

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be setting a firm weekly limit on how many jobs you accept and practicing a polite refusal, like offering the customer a later date or a small deposit to hold their slot instead of a false "tomorrow."

Both advisors miss it. The first says buy more machines, but even one machine can serve people well if the work is timed and stacked properly. The second says just say no and set a limit, but you cannot set a fair limit until you actually know how long each job takes.

**CAUSE:** The heart of your trouble is that you "promise too many people the same deadline" without knowing how many hours each dress, gomesi, or uniform batch really needs. You are guessing at dates instead of counting the actual sewing time and spacing the jobs out, so of course they collide. This is why honesty alone (just saying realistic dates) has not fixed it, you do not yet have the numbers to know what realistic means.

**PREDICTION:** If this is the cause, you will notice that the jobs that overrun are the ones you never timed, and you keep being surprised by how long a gomesi or a uniform bundle takes.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be writing down how many hours each type of garment truly takes, then giving every new customer a date based on the jobs already lined up ahead of theirs.

The problem is that his money sits idle in finished custom pieces because delivery-and-payment is the customer's decision, not his — without enforceable delivery deadlines or penalties, customers rationally delay because the finished furniture is already effectively theirs to collect whenever convenient.

raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** The trouble starts with your deposit. When a customer pays only a small deposit, you top it up with your own money to buy timber and start work, so most of the job is really funded by you. That means you carry all the risk while the customer has almost nothing at stake, which is exactly why they feel free to delay the balance for weeks or months.

**PREDICTION:** If this is the real problem, you should see that the customers who paid the smallest deposits are the same ones who drag out the final payment, while any customer who paid closer to half tends to collect and pay quickly.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be restructuring the deposit so the customer funds most of the job upfront, for example half before you buy timber and another chunk at the halfway mark. Frame it plainly, that timber is bought to their order, so their money, not just yours, must be in the wood.
